newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Storm clouds gather as Hong Kong handover nears.
newsitem.headline: Storm clouds gather as Hong Kong handover nears.

text.p: Hong Kong on Sunday approached its final two weeks as a British colony feverishly putting the finishing touches to the grand handover ceremonies while political storm clouds gathered on the horizon.
A diplomatic row is brewing between Britain and China which threatens to mar the historic red letter moment at midnight on June 30 when the colonial chapter ends and a new era dawns.
Hong Kong's democracy lobby fired off a salvo of criticism over laws drafted to tighten civil liberties after the handover, now just 16 days away.

Sino-British squabbles have rocked much of Hong Kong's drawn-out 13-year transition, launched in 1984 when then-Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher signed the accord under which Britain's last Asian possession would be returned to China.
But Hong Kong's 6.4 million residents are generally confident about their future as the end of 156 years of British rapidly approaches, opinion polls show.
Gloomy predictions of boarded up shop-fronts and a frantic last-minute exodus have proved wrong and an economic boom is underpinning an upbeat sense of well-being, the polls show.
Hong Kong people knighted and showered with awards in the latest British honours list celebrated openly on Saturday.
And on Sunday, Hong Kong was swept by a gambling frenzy as punters chasing the biggest pot ever wagered HK$400 million ($50 million) on the last horse races under British rule.

China in 1984 promised Hong Kong would retain its capitalist lifestyle and freedoms -- including gambling and horse-racing -- and opinion polls show Hong Kong people are on the whole willing to give Beijing the benefit of the doubt.
China, which regards the handover as the end of a century and a half of humiliation at British hands, announced last week that President Jiang Zemin would attend the handover ceremony.
Britain said new Prime Minister Tony Blair would accompany Prince Charles to the handover.

But festering political differences risk overshadowing the event. China and Britain locked horns last week over the Chinese section of the ceremony and Beijing's demands to send in troops of the future Chinese garrison while the British Union Jack was still flying.

The British flatly refused the troops request. They also plan to boycott the latter half of the grand handover ceremony when Beijing will inaugurate an unelected, post-handover legislature appointed by a China-approved panel in December.
Washington backed the British stance and Secretary of State Madeleine Albright will also shun the investiture ceremony.
But hopes of a united front from democratic nations crumbled when Australia, New Zealand and Japan, which have opposed the provisional legislature, declined to join ranks.
Meanwhile the provisional assembly further angered Hong Kong's democracy lobby by ramming through two laws on Saturday curbing political liberties and civil rights after the handover.
The 60-member assembly will be sworn in along with future leader, Tung Chee-hwa, his principle officials, and the judiciary in the early hours of July 1.
It will hold its first official meeting at 2.45 am (1845 GMT) to pass laws drafted in recent weeks in sessions held in China, provisional chamber president Rita Fan said on Sunday.
The laws curtail the rights of political parties and tighten police controls on protest marches. Western governments, especially the departing British, have denounced them.
"This is a clear sign of things to come," said Democratic Party leader Martin Lee, a vocal critic of the provisional chamber and the new laws.
Lee, whose party fared best in 1995 legislative elections said the changes "represent a step backwards for freedom and will revive colonial restrictions on basic rights".

As removal vans arrived at government house on Saturday to pack up the belongings of the 28th and last British Governor Chris Patten, the lights flashed on at the venue where the handover ceremonies will take place -- only to find a few holes in the roof still need to be plugged.

Workers have battled to complete Hong Kong's striking US$615 million waterfront hall in time for the opening and a charity banquet serving as a dress rehearsal for the gala dinner to be served to 4,000 international dignitaries invited to witness the historic handover.

The thunderstorms and torrential rains which have battered Hong Kong in recent days exposed one leak perilously close to the spot where the British flag will stand at the handover ceremony. But the builders, already working around the clock, confidentally predicted it would be all right on the night.
The government, meanwhile, is taking no chances. If it rains it will issue umbrellas to all the 10,000 guests expected to attend the celebrations.
